title: Universal temperature-dependent electrical resistivity in actinides
abstract: Temperature-dependent electrical resistivity $ρ(T)$ is one of the most common types of experimental data analyzed in condensed matter physics. For one group of pure metals, the actinides, experimental $ρ(T)$ curves differ radically from one another to the point that there is no unified theoretical approach to understanding and fitting $ρ(T)$ data in these elements. First-principles calculations result in $ρ(T)$ curves that differ from experimental data, even qualitatively. In an attempt to unravel this long-standing problem, here I propose a simple model that accurately fits the $ρ(T)$ data for eight phases of elemental actinides (from thorium (Th) to curium (Cm)) for which experimental data are publicly available to date. The model is based on the concept of two parallel conduction channels: one is described by the Bloch-Grüneisen equation, which is associated with the classical electron-phonon dissipation mechanism, and the other by the Arrhenius equation, which is associated with the nearest-neighbor hopping (NNH) conductivity. Debye temperatures $Θ_D$ derived from application of the model to $ρ(T)$ data for eight elemental actinide phases agree well with reported values deduced from heat capacity measurements. For neptunium (Np) a maximum Arrhenius activation energy (among all actinides) of $E_a=15.9$ $meV$ was derived. The model was also successfully applied to $ρ(T)$ data measured on $δ$-phase plutonium-based alloys Pu-Ce and Pu-Ce-Ga.
summary: This paper addresses the lack of a unified theory for understanding temperature-dependent electrical resistivity in actinides by proposing a two-channel parallel resistance model. The model combines an Arrhenius term (for nearest-neighbor hopping) with a Bloch-Grüneisen term (for electron-phonon scattering). By successfully fitting data across multiple actinide elements, it provides a quantitative framework for analyzing the complex electronic transport mechanisms in these materials.
main_problem: Experimental temperature-dependent electrical resistivity data for actinides are highly variable, lacking a unified theoretical approach for understanding and fitting these measurements.
main_result: The authors propose a model based on two parallel conduction channels (Arrhenius hopping and Bloch-Grüneisen) that successfully fits the $\rho(T)$ data for eight elemental actinide phases.
method: The resistivity is modeled as the reciprocal sum of conductivities from two distinct channels: one governed by Arrhenius behavior (NNH conductivity) and the other by electron-phonon scattering (Bloch-Grüneisen).
model_or_system: The system under study is pure elemental actinides (Th to Cm) and related alloys. The model, termed the NNH-parallel resistance model, treats total resistance as a parallel combination of two conduction channels: $\rho(T) = 1/(\sigma_{	ext{Arr}}(T) + \sigma_{	ext{BG}}(T))$.
key_observables: Temperature-dependent electrical resistivity ($\rho(T)$), Debye temperatures ($\Theta_D$), and Arrhenius activation energy ($E_a$).
important_parameters: Actinide elements (Th, Pa, U, Np, Pu); $E_a = 15.9$ meV for Np; $\Theta_D$ values consistent with heat capacity measurements.
main_assumptions: Matthiessen's rule is inapplicable for single-phase elemental metals, requiring the total resistance to be treated as a parallel combination of conduction channels.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate successful fits using the proposed model (Equation 10) across various actinide phases (Th, Pa, U, Np), comparing raw data against theoretical curves for both single-phase and multi-phase materials.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem of $\rho(T)$ variability in actinides. It then introduces the two-channel parallel resistance model ($\rho(T) = 1/(\sigma_{	ext{Arr}} + \sigma_{	ext{BG}})$). The core is applying and validating this model across multiple actinide elements, showing its success while noting specific parameters derived for each.
why_interesting: The study tackles the complex transport properties of actinides, which are quintessential examples of strongly correlated electron systems due to their partially filled $5f$ orbitals. Developing a successful empirical fit that incorporates both hopping and phonon mechanisms provides valuable physical insight into the underlying electronic structure.
